newsitem.title: THAILAND: Chavalit set to become new Thai premier.
newsitem.headline: Chavalit set to become new Thai premier.

text.p: Chavalit Yongchaiyudh, head of the New Aspiration Party (NAP) which won the most seats in last week's general election, is expected to be officially sworn in as Thailand's 22nd prime minister on Monday, officials said.
A royal decree officially nominating Chavalit to Thailand's top job should be issued late in the day, and King Bhumibol Adulyadej will likely then swear Chavalit in as the new premier.
"The royal decree appointing him to be Prime Minister should be announced later today," Bunchong Veesommai, Chavalit's personal secretary, told Reuters.

Usually the prime minister-designate waits one day after the royal decree is issued before he is sworn in, but the process is expected to be sped up so Chavalit can greet U.S. president Bill Clinton in his new capacity when he arrives for a brief state visit on Monday night.
"We hope it is all done before Clinton arrives," Bunchong said.
Clinton arrives at 9.30 p.m. (1430 GMT) for a brief visit -- the first U.S. presidential visit to Thailand in 27 years.
Outgoing prime minister Banharn Silpa-archa is currently representing Thailand in Manila at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

Chavalit's NAP won a slim two-seat victory over its rival Democrat Party in the November 17 general election. It has formed a six-party coalition which will command a comfortable majority of 221 seats in the 393-seat parliament.
Usually it takes about two weeks after the election before a new government is sworn in, according to usual procedure.
But the politicians have sped up the process and now all that remains is for the palace to issue the royal decree and the King to swear Chavalit in as new prime minister.
On Saturday the parliament elected deputy NAP leader Wan Muhamed Nor Matha as parliament president. His first duty was to forward Chavalit's name to the king for approval.
At the opening session of parliament, King Bhumibol urged the often-fractious parties to work together in the people's best interest.
The previous government led by Banharn lasted 14 months before he dissolved parliament in September following a bruising no-confidence debate, in which he was accused of corruption and mismanagement.
